blocks.text:
A URL shortener maps a long URL to a short code and redirects requests for the short URL to the long one. The problem looks trivial, and its value as a first case study lies in the fact that every decision is driven by numbers: the code length follows from the number of URLs, the cache size from the read skew, and the id generation scheme from the requirement that several servers create codes without coordinating on every request. The design below follows the seven-step framework of the first part of the book and uses `assumed` figures that are labelled as such; none of them is a measurement of a real service.

### Requirements and scope

**Functional requirements**

- Create a short URL for a long URL (`POST`), optionally with a custom alias and an expiry time.
- Redirect a request for a short URL to the original URL (`GET`), with low latency.
- Links expire at an optional deadline and can be deleted by their owner.
- Basic click analytics (count per link per day, coarse country) that must not slow down redirects.

**Non-functional requirements**

- Availability of the redirect path above 99.99% (assumed target): a dead link is visible to every end user of every page that embeds it.
- Redirect latency p99 below 100 ms inside the region (assumed), dominated by one cache lookup.
- Durability: an acknowledged short URL must never disappear.
- Codes must be short (at most 7 characters) and not trivially enumerable.
- Reads dominate writes by about 100 to 1 (assumed).

**Out of scope** are user accounts and billing, link-in-bio pages, QR code rendering, and malware scanning internals (only the hook is shown). **Assumptions**: one primary region with a second region for disaster recovery; the long URL is at most 2048 characters; links are immutable once created except for deletion.

### Capacity estimation

All inputs are assumptions. The arithmetic is shown so that a different input can be substituted.

rows: code 7 + URL about 100 + metadata about 150 + index overhead
20% of daily reads: 3,900 x 86,400 x 0.2 = 67 million entries x 300 bytes
blocks.caption: Capacity estimate for the URL shortener (all inputs assumed).

blocks.text:
Two conclusions follow. First, the data volume of 3 TB is small by distributed-database standards: sharding is chosen for write headroom and failure isolation more than for capacity. Second, 11,700 redirects per second is a modest load for a cache-backed service; the design effort concentrates on correctness, hot keys and the failure of the cache, not on raw throughput.

### API design

**REST API**

blocks.code:
POST /v1/urls
  body:   { "longUrl": "https://example.com/a/very/long/path?x=1",
            "alias": "spring-sale",        (optional, 4-20 chars [A-Za-z0-9_-])
            "expiresAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" }   (optional)
  header: Idempotency-Key: 7c2e...          (client generated, optional)
  201 Created  { "code": "aZ3k9Qx", "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/aZ3k9Qx" }
  409 Conflict      alias already taken
  422 Unprocessable URL invalid or blocked
  429 Too Many Requests   per-user creation limit exceeded

GET /{code}
  302 Found   Location: https://example.com/a/very/long/path?x=1
  404 Not Found   unknown or deleted code
  410 Gone        code existed and has expired

DELETE /v1/urls/{code}                  (owner only)   204 No Content
GET    /v1/urls/{code}/stats?from=&to=  200  { "clicks": [ {"day": "...", "n": 12} ] }
GET    /v1/urls?ownerId=&pageToken=&limit=50   cursor-based pagination

blocks.text:
The redirect uses 302 rather than 301 because a 301 may be cached by the browser indefinitely, which prevents click counting, expiry and deletion from taking effect. The trade-off is that every click reaches the service; this is acceptable at the estimated load. The `Idempotency-Key` header makes `POST` safe to retry: the service stores the key with the created code for 24 hours (assumed) and returns the same response for a repeated request. Pagination uses an opaque cursor (`pageToken`) instead of offsets, because offsets degrade on large partitions and shift when rows are inserted.

### Data model

The access pattern is a point lookup by code on the read path and an insert on the write path. There are no joins and no range scans on the hot path, which suits a key-value layout. A sharded relational store or a wide-column store both fit; the choice made here is a sharded, replicated relational store as covered in the databases material, with `code` as the partition key, because it gives unique constraints for custom aliases and simple operations.

blocks.text:
The custom alias shares the `code` column and namespace; its length (4 to 20) differs from generated codes (7), and a reserved-word list prevents aliases such as `api` or `admin`. The owner index is local to each shard, so listing the links of one owner is a scatter-gather query over all shards, which is acceptable because it is a rare dashboard operation and not a redirect.

### High-level architecture

blocks.text: **Create flow.** (1) The client sends `POST /v1/urls` through the load balancer. (2) The create service validates the URL (scheme `http` or `https`, length, blocklist) and normalises it. (3) If an alias was given, the service inserts it and maps a unique-key violation to 409. Otherwise it takes the next number from its in-memory range, permutes and encodes it as base62 (see the deep dive), and inserts the row. (4) The service writes the new entry into the cache and returns 201. The cache write is optional; it removes the cache miss of the first click. **Redirect flow.** (1) The redirect service looks up `url:{code}` in the cache. (2) On a hit it returns 302 immediately. (3) On a miss it reads the row from the owning shard, checks `expires_at`, populates the cache with a time to live of at most the remaining lifetime, and returns 302 or 404/410. (4) A click event is published to a queue after the response has been written; failure to publish never fails the redirect.

blocks.text:
### Deep dive

#### Problem 1: generating unique short codes

The design question is how several create servers produce codes that never collide, without a network round trip per code and without predictable output.

rows: Take a digest of the long URL, encode, keep 7 characters
Birthday collisions need a check and retry; the same URL by two users gets the same code
Acceptable for dedup, weak as the main scheme
Draw 7 random base62 characters; retry on unique-key violation
One failed insert per collision, rare at 0.17% fill; needs an insert round trip anyway
Simple and good at small fill
One atomic counter, encode the value
Counter is a bottleneck and a single point of failure; sequential codes are enumerable
Each server leases a block of 1,000 ids and counts locally
Gaps after a crash; sequential within a server
64 bits encode to 11 base62 characters, longer than 7
blocks.caption: Code generation alternatives.

blocks.text: The chosen scheme leases ranges from a counter row and then applies a keyed permutation so that consecutive numbers do not produce consecutive codes. The lease cost is one `UPDATE` per 1,000 creates; at the estimated 39 creates per second the counter row receives about 0.04 writes per second, which makes a single replicated database row sufficient.

blocks.text: The following program implements base62 encoding, range leasing, a Feistel permutation over 40 bits, and a measurement of collisions for the hash-and-truncate alternative with random values.

blocks.title: ShortCode.java

blocks.code:
$ java ShortCode.java
               0 -> 0        -> 0
              61 -> z        -> 61
              62 -> 10       -> 62
            3844 -> 100      -> 3844
      1000000000 -> 15ftgG   -> 1000000000
   3521614606207 -> zzzzzzz  -> 3521614606207
62^6 = 56800235584, 62^7 = 3521614606208
app server 1 leases [1, 1000]
app server 2 leases [1001, 2000]
app server 3 leases [2001, 3000]
sequential ids 1000001..1000004 -> plain / permuted
  4C93  /  1MFTHZF
  4C94  /  8fq2LU1
  4C95  /  7gcqHuo
  4C96  /  7TCgmtu
1,000,000 sequential ids -> distinct permuted values: 1000000
hash-truncation simulation (random values, fixed seed):
  5 chars (9.2e8 space), 100000 codes: 6 collisions
  7 chars (3.5e12 space), 5000000 codes: 5 collisions
  expected (n^2 / 2S): 5.5 and 3.5
blocks.title: Run ShortCode (JDK 21)

blocks.text:
**What to notice.** The largest 7-character code `zzzzzzz` decodes to 62^7 - 1 = 3,521,614,606,207, so the space is exactly as large as computed in the estimate. The permuted codes of consecutive ids share no visible pattern and remain unique for 1,000,000 consecutive inputs, because a Feistel network is a bijection whatever the round function is. The permutation is obfuscation, not encryption: it prevents casual enumeration but does not resist an attacker who learns the round constants, and a real deployment keeps the key secret. The collision simulation matches the birthday estimate n squared over 2S (6 observed against 5.5 expected for 5 characters, 5 observed against 3.5 expected for 7 characters, each a single run with a fixed seed), which is why hash-and-truncate always needs a collision check.

#### Problem 2: serving redirects fast and cheaply

With 3,900 reads per second on average and a skewed popularity distribution, a cache absorbs most of the load. Assuming a hit ratio of 90% (assumed, to be measured), the store sees about 390 reads per second on average and about 1,170 at peak, which a replicated store handles easily; the cache is nevertheless required for latency. The cache key is the code, the value is the long URL plus the expiry, and the time to live is `min(24 h, expires_at - now)`, so an expired link can never be served from the cache longer than its remaining lifetime.

#### Problem 3: expiry and deletion

Expiry is enforced lazily at read time (compare `expires_at` with the clock) and reclaimed eagerly by a background sweeper that deletes expired rows in small batches by partition. Deleting a link must also delete its cache entry; if that delete is lost, the entry still expires by its time to live. Codes of deleted or expired links are not reused for a retention period (assumed 1 year), because a reused code would silently redirect old embedded links to a new destination.

### Bottlenecks, failures and real-world problems

#### Viral link creates a hot key

**Scenario.** A link is shared by a popular account and receives 150,000 requests per second, about 13 times the estimated peak load of the whole service. **Symptoms.** One cache node shows saturated CPU and rising latency while the other nodes are idle; redirect p99 rises for every code that hashes to the same node.

**Diagnosis.** Per-key request counters or the cache's hot-key statistics show a single key dominating; the node's network card or single-threaded command loop is the limit. **Root cause.** Consistent hashing or slot assignment places each key on one node, so the capacity of a single key is the capacity of a single node, regardless of cluster size.

**Fix.** Add a small in-process cache (a few thousand entries, 1 to 5 seconds time to live) in each redirect instance so that at most one request per instance per second reaches the cache for the hot code; allow the CDN to cache the 302 for a few seconds for links flagged as hot (`Cache-Control: public, max-age=5`). **Prevention.** Keep the in-process layer enabled by default, track per-key rates, and load-test with a Zipf-skewed key distribution instead of a uniform one.

#### Cold cache after a cache cluster failure

**Scenario.** The cache cluster restarts after a failed deployment and every entry is gone. **Symptoms.** The store receives 3,900 reads per second instead of 390; its latency rises, the connection pool saturates, and redirects time out, which triggers client retries and more load.

**Diagnosis.** Cache hit ratio drops to zero in the dashboard at the same time as store read latency and queue depth rise. **Root cause.** The store was sized for the miss rate, not for the full read rate, so the system depended on the cache for availability and not only for latency.

**Fix.** Coalesce concurrent misses for the same code into one store read (single flight), cap concurrent store reads per instance and return 503 with `Retry-After` above the cap, and warm the cache from the most recent top-N list before putting a restarted cache back in rotation. **Prevention.** Size the store for the cold-start read rate or provide admission control that protects it, and rehearse a cache loss in a game day.

#### Counter row unavailable or range exhausted

**Scenario.** The database holding `id_ranges` fails over for 40 seconds while a server consumes its last ids. **Symptoms.** `POST /v1/urls` fails with 5xx on that server only; other servers are unaffected until their ranges also run out.

**Diagnosis.** Lease errors in the logs; the per-server remaining-range gauge reaches zero. **Root cause.** The server leased lazily, so a short outage of the allocator became an outage of creation.

**Fix.** Prefetch the next range when 10% of the current range remains, and keep a lease large enough to cover several minutes of peak traffic (1,000 ids last 25 seconds at 39 per second, so the step is raised to 100,000 for production, assumed). **Prevention.** Alert on remaining range per server, accept gaps in the code space, and never let the allocator be on the redirect path.

#### Abuse: phishing and spam links

**Scenario.** Attackers create thousands of short links that point to phishing pages. **Symptoms.** Spike in creation from few accounts; user reports; the domain appears on a blocklist of a browser vendor.

**Diagnosis.** Group creations by owner, IP range and destination domain; compare destinations against a reputation feed. **Root cause.** A shortener hides the destination, which makes it attractive for abuse, and creation had no per-user limit. **Fix.** Apply creation rate limits per user and per IP (see the rate limiter design), check the destination against a reputation service before insert, allow takedown by setting a `blocked` flag that the redirect returns as an interstitial page. **Prevention.** Require sign-in above a creation threshold, and review the highest-volume destinations periodically.

### Trade-offs and extensions

- **Multi-region.** Replicate the URL store asynchronously to a second region; reads are served locally, writes go to the primary region. A lag of a few seconds means a link created in one region may return 404 in the other for that time; mitigate by writing the new entry into the cache of both regions at creation.
- **Cache versus CDN.** A CDN can serve 302 responses at the edge and cut latency further, at the price of delayed deletion and lost click counts for cached responses; use it only for hot links.
- **Custom domains.** Add a `domain` column to the key (`domain + code`), and look up by host header.
- **Analytics accuracy.** The queue-based pipeline gives at-least-once delivery, so counts are approximate unless events carry unique ids and the aggregation deduplicates them.

### Questions to expect

#### Why base62 and not base64?

Base64 includes `+` and `/`, which need escaping in URLs, and the URL-safe variant adds `-` and `_`, which look ambiguous in some fonts and are valid in aliases. Base62 uses only letters and digits, and its density (5.95 bits per character) is close to base64 (6 bits).

#### How many characters are required for 6 billion URLs?

62^6 = 5.7e10 already exceeds 6.0e9, so 6 characters suffice with 10.6% of the space used. Seven characters (3.5e12) leave a margin and make random generation collide rarely, and so 7 is chosen.

#### 301 or 302?

302, because every click must pass through the service for analytics, expiry and deletion. A 301 reduces load but the browser may cache it permanently and later changes are invisible. 301 suits permanent, non-tracked redirects.

#### How are collisions handled with random codes?

The insert uses the primary key as the arbiter. A unique-key violation triggers a retry with a new random code, up to a small limit. At 0.17% fill the expected number of retries per create is 0.0017.

#### How does the design scale to ten times the traffic?

Redirects scale horizontally with more stateless instances and cache nodes; the store gains read replicas first and shards second. The allocator is not on the hot path, and its lease step increases from 1,000 to larger values.

#### What happens when two users shorten the same URL?

Each receives a different code by default, which keeps analytics and ownership separate. Deduplication by `url_hash` is an option for anonymous links, at the price of sharing deletion semantics.

#### How is the availability of the redirect path protected?

Stateless instances in several zones, a replicated cache with a local in-process layer, a replicated store with read replicas, and admission control that sheds load before the store collapses. Creation can fail without affecting redirects.

#### How would custom aliases change the design?

They share the namespace, so uniqueness is enforced by the same primary key; reserved words are blocked, and a creation returns 409 on conflict. Aliases are not generated, so they bypass the range allocator.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- The numbers drive the design: 6.0 billion codes need 6 characters, 7 give a safe margin, and 3 TB of data fits a few shards.
- Range allocation removes the counter from the hot path; a crash causes gaps, never duplicates.
- A keyed permutation hides the sequence; it is obfuscation and not a security boundary.
- Use 302 when clicks, expiry and deletion matter; protect the store from a cold cache and the cache from a hot key.
- Keep analytics asynchronous so that a slow pipeline never slows a redirect.

A rate limiter bounds how many requests a client may make in a period. It protects services from overload and abuse, enforces fairness between tenants, and implements commercial plans. The algorithms were compared in the part on common infrastructure components; this chapter designs the service around them: where the check runs, where the counters live, how rules reach the checkers, and what happens when the counter store fails. The central difficulty is that a limit of 100 requests per minute for a user must hold even though the user's requests arrive at many gateway instances.

### Requirements and scope

**Functional requirements**

- Decide for each request whether it is allowed, using rules that match on subject (user, API key, IP address, tenant), endpoint and method.
- Support several algorithms per rule (token bucket for burst-tolerant APIs, sliding window counter for strict windows).
- Return the decision with remaining quota and retry time so that clients can back off: `429 Too Many Requests`, `Retry-After`, and the `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers.
- Rules are changed at runtime without a deployment.

**Non-functional requirements**

- Added latency below 5 ms at p99 (assumed); the check is on the critical path of every request.
- High availability: the limiter must never become the reason an API is down.
- Accuracy: an over-admission of a few percent is acceptable; under-admission (blocking legitimate traffic) is worse.
- Memory efficiency per key, because the number of keys is large.

**Out of scope** are the billing integration, DDoS mitigation at the network layer (handled by the edge), and client-side throttling. **Assumptions**: the limiter runs in the API gateway tier; the counter store is an in-memory key-value store with atomic server-side scripts (a Redis cluster, as covered in the Redis material); keys are identified by an authenticated subject or by IP when anonymous.

### Capacity estimation

blocks.caption: Capacity estimate for the rate limiter (all inputs assumed).

blocks.text:
The comparison of 2 GB against 160 GB is the reason sliding window logs are reserved for small limits, and the shard count follows from operation rate and not from memory.

### API design

The limiter is consumed in two ways: embedded as a filter in the gateway, which calls the counter store directly, or as a standalone decision service that other services call. The decision API is small.

**Decision API (gRPC style, shown as REST)**

A denied decision still returns HTTP 200 from the decision API; the gateway turns it into a 429 response for the end client. A `cost` greater than 1 supports weighted endpoints (an export counts as 10).

### Data model

blocks.code:
rules:
  - id: orders-read
    match: { path: "/v1/orders/**", method: GET }
    subject: user                  # user | api_key | ip | tenant
    algorithm: token_bucket
    capacity: 20                   # burst size
    refill_per_second: 10          # sustained rate
    on_store_failure: local        # open | closed | local
  - id: login
    match: { path: "/v1/login", method: POST }
    subject: ip
    algorithm: sliding_window_counter
    limit: 5
    window_seconds: 60
    on_store_failure: closed       # security rules fail closed
blocks.title: rules.yaml

blocks.text:
Counters live in the store as one hash per subject and rule: key `rl:{ruleId}:{subject}` with fields `tokens` and `ts` (last refill time in milliseconds), and an expiry set to twice the time needed to refill from empty, so that idle keys disappear on their own. The store is partitioned by key hash, and all fields of one key live on one shard, which is what makes a single-key atomic script possible. Rules are a small document set kept in a configuration store; gateways cache them and refresh every 30 seconds (assumed) or on a change notification.

### High-level architecture

blocks.text: **Request flow.** (1) The gateway authenticates the request and derives the subject. (2) It selects the matching rules from its local rule cache. (3) For each rule it sends one script call to the shard that owns `rl:{ruleId}:{subject}`. (4) If all rules allow, the request is forwarded; otherwise the gateway returns 429 with `Retry-After`. Calls to different shards for the two rules are issued in parallel to keep the added latency at one round trip.

blocks.title: RateLimit.java

blocks.code:
$ java RateLimit.java
burst of 20 requests across a window boundary, limit 10 per 10 s
  fixed window   accepted: 20
  sliding log    accepted: 10
  sliding counter accepted: 11
  token bucket   accepted: 10
token bucket (capacity 20, 5/s): steady accepted 300 of 300, burst after idle accepted 20 of 30
global limit 90/s, offered 80+10+10 = 100/s
  central counter accepts 90/s
  3 local limiters of 30/s accept 50/s (the limit allows 90/s)
blocks.title: Run RateLimit (JDK 21)

blocks.text:
**What to notice.** The fixed window admits twice the limit across the boundary. The sliding window counter admits 11 in this run because it estimates the previous window by weighting, an approximation that errs by a small amount in this adversarial pattern. The token bucket with capacity 10 and refill of 1 token per second admits exactly the initial 10 and then refills slowly; after 20 idle seconds it holds its capacity of 20 and admits 20 of an instant burst of 30. The last two lines show why a per-node split of a global limit is not equivalent to a central count: when the load balancer sends 80% of a user's traffic to one of three gateways, three local limiters of 30 per second accept only 50 per second although 90 are allowed.

#### Problem 2: atomicity of the check

A limiter that reads the counter, compares it with the limit and writes it back in separate network calls admits too many requests under concurrency, because two gateways read the same value before either writes. The atomic variant performs the whole decision in one server-side step. The simulation below reproduces the effect with threads: each check-then-set read is followed by a 20 microsecond pause, which stands in for a network round trip.

blocks.title: RaceDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java RaceDemo.java
limit = 100, 4000 attempts
round 1: check-then-set admitted 797, atomic admitted 100
round 2: check-then-set admitted 799, atomic admitted 100
round 3: check-then-set admitted 762, atomic admitted 100
blocks.title: Run RaceDemo (JDK 21; timing dependent, typical output)

blocks.text:
The check-then-set version admitted roughly eight times the limit, and the atomic version admitted exactly 100 in every round. The same applies to a store: use a single atomic command (`INCR` with an expiry set on the first increment) or a server-side script. The token bucket in Redis is implemented as a script (shown for illustration; it was not run, because no Redis server is available on the build machine):

**token\_bucket.lua (not run)**

blocks.code:
-- KEYS[1] = rl:{ruleId}:{subject}
-- ARGV: capacity, refill per second, now in ms (from the gateway), cost
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate     = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now      = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local cost     = tonumber(ARGV[4])
local d = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(d[1])
local ts     = tonumber(d[2])
if tokens == nil then tokens = capacity; ts = now end
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + math.max(0, now - ts) * rate / 1000)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost; allowed = 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity / rate * 2000))
return { allowed, tostring(tokens) }

blocks.text:
A script runs on the single command thread of one shard without interleaving, so the read-modify-write is atomic. The gateway supplies the time, so clocks of different gateways must be synchronised within a few milliseconds; an alternative is to read the store's own clock inside the script, at the cost of a dependency on the script replication mode of the server version in use.

#### Problem 3: distributed accuracy versus cost

rows: Central store, one call per request
One round trip per request; store failure needs a policy
Local counters, limit divided by N
Poor when load is uneven (50 of 90 per second above)
Sticky routing by subject, local counters
Breaks on instance loss and rebalancing
Token leasing: gateways take batches of tokens centrally and spend locally
Over-admission bounded by (instances x batch size)
One call per batch; hot keys become cheap
blocks.caption: Where the count lives.

blocks.text:
The design uses the central store as the default and token leasing for subjects whose rate exceeds a threshold (for example 5,000 requests per second), where a single key would otherwise put the whole load of one subject on one shard.

### Bottlenecks, failures and real-world problems

#### Counter store outage turns into a platform outage

**Scenario.** One counter shard fails over; for 30 seconds calls to it time out after the default 2 seconds. **Symptoms.** Gateway threads are blocked on the limiter, request latency rises to the timeout for every user whose key lives on that shard (one eighth of users), gateway connection pools fill and unrelated endpoints slow down.

**Diagnosis.** Latency histograms of the limiter call show a step at the timeout value; gateway thread dumps show threads waiting on the store client. **Root cause.** The limiter was treated as a mandatory dependency with a long timeout and no failure policy, which made a protection component into a source of cascading failure.

**Fix.** Set a 10 ms timeout without retries, open a circuit breaker after a few consecutive failures, and apply the per-rule policy: login and payment rules fail closed, general API rules fail to a local limiter (limit divided by instance count) so that the system degrades to approximate limiting instead of none. **Prevention.** Alert on breaker state and on the share of decisions made in degraded mode, and rehearse a store failure.

blocks.text:
#### Over-admission because of a non-atomic check

**Scenario.** A new implementation reads the counter with `GET`, compares it and writes with `SET`. **Symptoms.** Customers with bursts of parallel requests exceed their limit by a factor of several; the effect disappears in single-threaded tests.

**Diagnosis.** Replaying 8 parallel clients against a staging limiter reproduces over-admission (as in the RaceDemo run above). **Root cause.** Read-modify-write over the network is not atomic.

**Fix.** Use one atomic command or a server-side script for the complete decision. **Prevention.** Include a concurrent test in the build that asserts the admitted count never exceeds the limit.

#### One tenant saturates one shard

**Scenario.** A large customer sends 60,000 requests per second under one API key. **Symptoms.** The shard owning that key reaches 100% CPU on its command thread; other keys on the same shard see timeouts.

**Diagnosis.** Per-key operation counters (sampling of the command stream) show one key with 75% of the shard's operations. **Root cause.** All decisions for a key land on one shard, so one key is limited by the capacity of one shard, 80,000 checks per second in the estimate.

**Fix.** Switch the key to token leasing: each gateway instance obtains a batch of tokens (for example 5% of the per-second limit) and spends them locally, calling the store once per batch. **Prevention.** Detect keys above a rate threshold automatically and move them to leasing; accept that over-admission is bounded by instances times batch size.

#### False positives behind shared IP addresses

**Scenario.** A limit of 100 requests per minute per IP blocks every user in a company or on a mobile carrier gateway. **Symptoms.** Many users report 429 from the same address range while their individual usage is low.

**Diagnosis.** The blocked requests carry different user identifiers but the same source address. **Root cause.** The IP address was used as the identity for authenticated traffic, though many users can share one address.

**Fix.** Limit authenticated traffic by user or API key, and keep IP rules only for anonymous endpoints with high limits. **Prevention.** Choose the subject from the identity that the business wants to limit, and review IP rules for NAT effects.

### Trade-offs and extensions

- **Fail open versus fail closed.** A limiter that fails open may let a flood through during an outage, one that fails closed turns its own failure into an outage; the decision belongs to each rule and is recorded in it.
- **Placement.** An edge or CDN limit protects the whole platform cheaply but sees little identity; a gateway limit knows the user; a service-level limit knows the cost of each operation. Layers are complementary.
- **Dynamic limits.** Adaptive concurrency limits that follow observed latency complement fixed quotas by protecting against overload that no fixed number predicts.
- **Multi-region.** Each region enforces its share of a global quota, with periodic rebalancing; exact global limits across regions cost a cross-region round trip per request and are rarely worth it.

### Questions to expect

#### Which algorithm would be chosen for a public API and why?

A token bucket, because it permits short bursts that real clients produce and constrains the sustained rate, and because it needs two numbers per key. A sliding window counter is chosen when the contract is a strict count per window.

#### How is the limiter made accurate across many gateway instances?

All instances consult the same counter through an atomic script, so the count is exact per key. The cost is one round trip per request, which is reduced by leasing batches of tokens for very hot keys.

#### What happens when Redis is unavailable?

A short timeout and a circuit breaker prevent the limiter from slowing requests. Each rule defines its policy: fail closed for sensitive operations, otherwise degrade to local limits of limit divided by instance count, and alert.

#### How does the fixed window counter fail?

A client can send the full limit just before and just after the boundary, which is twice the limit within a short time. The sliding window counter or the token bucket removes the cliff.

#### How are rules changed without redeploying?

Gateways cache the rule set and refresh it on a timer or on a change notification. Changes are versioned so that a bad rule can be rolled back, and a new rule can be applied in shadow mode (decisions logged, not enforced) first.

#### How is clock skew between gateways handled?

Use the store's clock inside the script where the server version allows it, or keep the gateway clocks synchronised with NTP and make the algorithm tolerant by using `max(0, now - ts)` so that a small backwards step never produces negative refill.

#### How many shards are needed for 400,000 checks per second?

Divide by the benchmarked capacity per shard. With an assumed 80,000 checks per second, five shards are the minimum and eight keep utilisation near 60%, which leaves room for a shard failing over.

#### How would a limit per tenant across all its users be implemented?

Add a second rule with the tenant as the subject, evaluated in the same request. The tenant key is hot by construction, so it uses token leasing.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- The decision must be one atomic step: a server-side script or a single command, never read-then-write.
- A token bucket suits most APIs; a fixed window can admit twice the limit across a boundary.
- A per-node split of a global limit under-admits when load is uneven; use a central count, plus token leasing for hot keys.
- Decide per rule whether the limiter fails open, closed or local, set a 10 ms timeout, and use a circuit breaker.
- Size the shard count from the operation rate (about 80,000 checks per second per shard, assumed), not from memory.

Distributed systems need identifiers that are unique without asking a single database for every one. A relational auto-increment column does not survive sharding, a random UUID is large and ruins index locality, and a global counter service is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. This chapter designs an id service for 64-bit identifiers that are unique across machines, roughly ordered by creation time, and generated without a network call per id. The embedded Snowflake implementation of the earlier chapter on distributed coordination is the starting point; here the focus is the service around it: assigning worker ids, handling clocks, the alternative of segment allocation, and the failures that cause duplicates.

### Requirements and scope

**Functional requirements**

- Return globally unique 64-bit ids, one at a time or in batches.
- Ids are roughly time-ordered (k-sortable): ids created later are larger, within the clock accuracy.
- Ids fit in a signed 64-bit integer (a `BIGINT` column and a Java `long`).

**Non-functional requirements**

- Throughput of 100,000 ids per second in total (assumed peak), with spare capacity.
- Latency below 5 ms at p99 over the network (assumed), or zero when embedded as a library.
- No single point of failure; a node failure must not stop id generation.
- Uniqueness is mandatory; order is best effort.

**Out of scope**: gapless sequences (for example invoice numbers, which need a transactional counter), strict global ordering (which needs a consensus log), and ids that must be unguessable (use random tokens). **Assumptions**: node clocks are synchronised by NTP to within tens of milliseconds, and nodes are restarted from time to time.

### Capacity estimation

rows: 10 billion rows x 8 bytes against 16 bytes
blocks.caption: Capacity estimate for the id generator (inputs assumed).

blocks.text:
Throughput is not the constraint: one node could serve the entire load. The number of nodes follows from availability and from the geographic spread of callers.

### API design

**API**

blocks.code:
GET /v1/ids?count=100
  200 { "ids": ["4194455552", "4194455553", ...] }     ids as decimal strings
gRPC: rpc NextIds(NextIdsRequest{count}) returns (NextIdsResponse{repeated int64 ids})

blocks.text:
Ids are returned as strings over JSON because JavaScript numbers are IEEE 754 doubles that represent integers exactly only up to 2^53 (about 9.0e15), and a Snowflake id uses up to 63 bits. A client that parses the id as a number silently rounds it. The gRPC variant uses a native 64-bit integer.

### Data model

The generator holds almost no persistent data, which is the point of the design. The only shared state is the assignment of worker ids.

rows: node address, lease TTL 30 s, heartbeat every 10 s
Exclusive worker id for a running node (registry)
Refuse or wait after a restart when the clock is earlier
Segment allocation: one row per id space

blocks.text: **Start-up.** A node acquires a lease on a free worker id in the registry (an ephemeral key with a time to live that the node refreshes), loads its persisted `last_ts` and refuses to serve until the clock has passed it. **Generation.** A request is handled entirely in memory: read the clock, compare with the last timestamp, increment the sequence or reset it, and compose the id. **Failure.** If a node loses its lease (network partition from the registry), it stops generating before the lease can expire for another holder; this is the rule that prevents two nodes from running with the same worker id.

blocks.text:
### Deep dive

#### Problem 1: choosing the scheme

rows: One writer; sharding needs offsets; the database is on the path of every insert
Ticket server (two databases, odd and even)
Servers are a dependency; order only within each server
Ranges leased from a table; local counting
Gaps after a crash; ids are not time-ordered across servers
16 bytes; random inserts fragment B-tree indexes
Needs worker ids and a trustworthy clock
blocks.caption: Id generation alternatives.

blocks.text:
#### Problem 2: assigning worker ids safely

A static configuration file is simple but fails when a virtual machine image is cloned or a container is rescheduled with the same configuration; two nodes with worker id 17 produce identical ids whenever they generate in the same millisecond with the same sequence. A lease in a coordination service assigns each running node a unique worker id; the lease time to live must exceed the largest tolerated clock difference and pause (garbage collection, VM freeze), so that a node that was frozen cannot resume while another node already holds its id. A frozen node must check its lease before every batch, not only at start.

#### Problem 3: clocks

The timestamp must never decrease for a given worker. A clock can move backwards through an NTP step, a manual change, a virtual machine migration or a leap second. The safe policy is to remember the last issued timestamp, and when the clock reads less, either wait (for steps of a few milliseconds) or refuse (for large steps) and raise an alert, as the program below does. Prefer clock slewing to stepping in the NTP configuration, and use a monotonic clock for measuring elapsed time within the process while anchoring it once to the wall clock at start.

blocks.title: Run IdGen (JDK 21)

blocks.text:
**What to notice.** The decoded id shows the three fields. Ten thousand ids were generated when the clock advanced slower than 4,096 ids per millisecond; the generator waited twice for the next millisecond (overflow waits) and the ids stayed strictly increasing. A rollback of 3 ms was absorbed by staying on the last timestamp, a rollback of 40 ms raised an error. The segment allocator served 10,500 ids with 12 database round trips (including one prefetched segment that was not yet used), and after a restart it started at 12,001: the unused part of the old segment is a gap, but no id is reused.

### Bottlenecks, failures and real-world problems

#### Duplicate ids from two nodes with the same worker id

**Scenario.** A deployment template copies the worker id 17 to a second instance during a scale-out. **Symptoms.** Unique-key violations on inserts, appearing only under load and only for rows created in the same millisecond by different nodes.

**Diagnosis.** Decode the colliding ids: identical timestamp and worker fields, different callers. **Root cause.** Worker ids were assigned by configuration instead of an exclusive lease.

**Fix.** Acquire worker ids from the registry with a lease, and refuse to start without one. **Prevention.** Log the worker id on every node at start and alert on two nodes with the same value; test cloned images in staging.

#### Clock steps backwards after a time synchronisation

**Scenario.** An NTP daemon steps the clock back 40 ms after a long drift. **Symptoms.** Ids go out of order; if the generator has no guard, ids are duplicated when the clock passes the old range again.

**Diagnosis.** Compare the generation log with the system log of the time daemon; find the step event at the same instant. **Root cause.** Wall-clock time is not monotonic.

**Fix.** Persist the last timestamp, wait for small rollbacks and refuse for large ones, and have the node report unhealthy so that the load balancer removes it. **Prevention.** Configure slewing instead of stepping, monitor clock offset, and alert above a threshold of a few milliseconds.

#### Sequence overflow under a burst

**Scenario.** A batch job asks one node for 50,000 ids inside a single millisecond. **Symptoms.** Latency of the batch increases in steps of one millisecond.

**Diagnosis.** The overflow-wait counter rises. **Root cause.** The sequence is 12 bits, so at most 4,096 ids per millisecond per node are available.

**Fix.** Wait for the next millisecond when the sequence overflows (the demo shows two waits for 10,000 ids when the clock is slow), spread large batches over several nodes, or give callers a block of ids to use locally. **Prevention.** Size the worker-bit and sequence-bit split for the peak burst, and measure the overflow counter.

#### Large ids corrupted in a browser

**Scenario.** A web page displays order id 4198649857 correctly but id 1802389301384290305 differently from the server value. **Symptoms.** Clicking a link opens the wrong order or a 404; the last digits of the id differ.

**Diagnosis.** Compare the JSON text with the value in the JavaScript console. **Root cause.** The JSON number was parsed as an IEEE 754 double, which is exact only up to 2^53.

**Fix.** Serialise ids as strings in APIs consumed by JavaScript. **Prevention.** Contract tests with ids above 2^53, and a lint rule for `long` fields in public schemas.

### Trade-offs and extensions

- **Time-ordered versus unguessable.** Time-ordered ids leak creation time and, through the sequence, approximate volume; where this matters, expose a separate public token and keep the Snowflake id internal.
- **Bit layout.** The 10 + 12 split can be changed (for example 8 worker bits and 14 sequence bits) to match the number of nodes and the burst size; once ids exist the layout is fixed.
- **Epoch.** The custom epoch should be a recent date, because 41 bits last 69.7 years from it; moving the epoch later would only be possible with a new id format.
- **Embedding.** The generator can run in each application process with worker ids from the registry, which removes the network hop and the service, at the price of a larger registry and worker-id space.

### Questions to expect

#### Why not use UUIDs?

A random UUID is 128 bits and its randomness spreads inserts over the whole index, which causes page splits and poor cache locality in a B-tree. A time-ordered 64-bit id appends at the right edge of the index and halves the key size. UUID v7 repairs the ordering but keeps 128 bits.

#### How does the generator guarantee uniqueness?

Three fields make an id unique: the timestamp, the exclusive worker id and the per-millisecond sequence. Uniqueness holds as long as worker ids are exclusive and the timestamp never decreases for a worker.

#### What happens if the clock moves backwards?

The generator compares the clock with its last timestamp; it waits for small differences, refuses for larger ones and reports unhealthy, so that duplicates are impossible. Operations avoid clock steps through slewing.

#### How many ids can one node issue per second?

4,096 per millisecond, which is 4,096,000 per second with 12 sequence bits. Overflow waits for the next millisecond.

#### What is the difference between this and segment allocation?

Segment allocation hands ranges of numbers from a database to servers, which count locally. It needs no clock and gives dense numbers, but ids are not time-ordered across servers and a crash leaves gaps. Snowflake needs a clock and worker ids and is naturally k-sortable.

#### How are ids made unique across regions?

Worker ids are drawn from one registry that is global, or the worker bits are split into region and node parts (for example 3 plus 7 bits), so that each region assigns its own range without coordination.

#### Can ids be strictly ordered?

Not without a single sequencer or consensus. Snowflake ids are ordered per worker and approximately across workers within the clock error. Systems needing a strict total order use a consensus log, at the price of throughput and latency.

#### What breaks after 69.7 years?

The 41-bit timestamp overflows; by choosing a recent custom epoch the lifetime starts at that date. A migration to a new format would be needed long before that.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- 64 bits split into 41 time, 10 worker, 12 sequence give 4,096 ids per millisecond per node and 69.7 years of time.
- Uniqueness depends on exclusive worker ids (use leases, never copied configuration) and on a timestamp that never decreases.
- Wait for small clock rollbacks, refuse large ones, and configure time daemons to slew instead of step.
- Return 64-bit ids as strings to JavaScript clients; numbers above 2^53 are corrupted.
- Segment allocation trades ordering for simplicity: no clock, dense numbers, gaps after a crash.

A notification system delivers messages to users through push notifications, SMS and email on behalf of many producing services: one-time passwords, order updates, security alerts and marketing campaigns. The problem is not sending a message; it is sending the right message exactly once from the user's point of view, through unreliable third-party providers, with the urgent messages never waiting behind the bulk ones, and with respect for the user's preferences. The design is built on a message queue (as covered in the part on asynchronous processing) and uses idempotency, retries with backoff, priority isolation and per-provider rate limiting as its core mechanisms.

### Requirements and scope

**Functional requirements**

- Accept a notification request from internal services (API or event) and deliver it on one or more channels: mobile push, SMS, email.
- Priorities: critical (one-time passwords, security alerts), transactional (order and payment updates), bulk (marketing, digests).
- Templates with localisation; user preferences per channel and type (opt-out, quiet hours).
- Scheduled and campaign notifications (one message to a segment of 20 million users).
- Delivery status tracking: queued, sent, delivered, failed, with provider callbacks.
- No duplicates in normal operation, and retries for transient provider errors.

**Non-functional requirements**

- Critical messages are delivered within 5 seconds at p99 (assumed), independent of bulk load.
- At-least-once delivery inside the system, effectively once for the user through deduplication.
- High availability of intake: a producer must be able to hand over a message even when providers are down.
- Provider rate limits and cost (SMS is the most expensive channel) are respected.

**Out of scope**: in-app inbox UI, the content of marketing segmentation, A/B experimentation, and the internals of the providers. **Assumptions**: 100 million notifications per day; third-party providers for each channel; a message broker with partitions.

### Capacity estimation

rows: about 5,600 per second, on top of the average
peak push 6,000; email 4,800; SMS 1,200 per second
a campaign of 20,000,000 x 1 KB enqueued at once
blocks.caption: Capacity estimate for the notification system (inputs assumed).

blocks.text:
Two conclusions drive the architecture. The volume is moderate, so the problem is not throughput but isolation: a campaign that takes an hour to drain must not delay a one-time password. And the log is large enough (4.5 TB) to be a partitioned store, not a single database.

### API design

**REST API**

blocks.code:
POST /v1/notifications
  headers: Idempotency-Key: order-9981-shipped        (required, 24 h dedup window)
  body: { "userId": 42, "type": "order_shipped", "priority": "transactional",

blocks.text:
The response `202 Accepted` states honestly that delivery is asynchronous. The idempotency key makes retries by producers harmless: a repeated request returns the original id and does not create a second notification.

blocks.text:
The notification log is written once per message and updated as status changes; reads are by id and by user (inbox and support views). A wide-column store or a sharded relational store partitioned by `user_id` fits; the status field is updated by workers and callbacks, so updates must be idempotent and ordered by status rank (a late `sent` never overwrites a `delivered`). The `idempotency_key` has a unique index (or a dedup key in a cache with a 24-hour time to live in front of it) to reject duplicates quickly.

blocks.caption: Intake is separated from delivery by queues; a router applies preferences and templates and fans out to per-channel queues, where workers enforce provider limits, retry, and send failures to a dead-letter queue.

blocks.text:
**Intake flow.** (1) The API authenticates the producer, validates the request and checks the idempotency key (`SET key` `NX` with a 24-hour time to live; if the key exists, the existing id is returned). (2) It writes the notification record and publishes it to the intake topic for its priority; only then does it answer `202`. (3) Events from other systems (order created) enter the same way through a consumer that calls the same code path.

**Routing.** The router consumes the intake topics, loads user preferences and device tokens, suppresses messages the user opted out of, defers bulk messages during quiet hours, renders the template with the parameters in the user's language, and publishes one message per chosen channel to that channel's queue. Preferences are read at send time and not at intake, so an opt-out takes effect even for messages that have waited in a queue.

**Delivery.** Channel workers consume their queue, take a token from the provider-level rate limiter, call the provider with a request id that the provider can use for its own deduplication, record the attempt, and acknowledge the queue message. Transient errors schedule a retry; fatal errors (invalid address, unregistered device token) mark the message failed without retry and update the device or address record.

blocks.text:
### Deep dive

#### Problem 1: priorities without starvation

A single queue is first-in first-out: 20 million campaign messages enqueued at 08:00 delay a password reset requested at 08:01 by more than an hour. Brokers such as Kafka do not provide message priorities within a partition, so priority is implemented by separating the traffic.

rows: Not available in every broker; hard to partition
Separate queues per priority, workers drain high first
Dedicated consumers or a strict-priority poll loop
Low priority can starve under sustained high load
Chosen with a share for low
blocks.caption: Priority alternatives.

blocks.text: The simulation below sends 2,000 promotional messages at time 0 and 20 one-time passwords during the first 10 seconds, with a provider that accepts 50 messages per second and fails transiently 20% of the time. It also submits 30 duplicate promotional requests (same dedup key) and retries failures with exponential backoff and full jitter up to 5 attempts.

blocks.code:
$ java NotifySim.java
2000 promotional + 20 OTP messages + 30 duplicate submissions;
provider limit 50/s, 20% transient failures
single FIFO queue          delivered=2019 retries=455 dead=1 duplicates suppressed=30
                           OTP latency (s): p50=36 max=48; queue empty at t=68 s
priority queues (HIGH first) delivered=2019 retries=454 dead=1 duplicates suppressed=30

blocks.text:
**What to notice.** With a single FIFO queue the one-time passwords wait a median of 36 seconds and a maximum of 48 seconds behind the promotional backlog; with priority ordering the median is 0 and the maximum 1 second, and the total time to drain everything is nearly the same (68 and 69 seconds), so priority changes who waits without costing throughput. The 30 duplicate submissions were suppressed. About 455 retries happened for 2,020 messages, in line with a 20% failure rate, and one message exhausted its 5 attempts and was dead-lettered; the probability of that for a message is 0.2 to the power 5, which is 0.032%, and 2,020 messages at that rate give about 0.65 expected dead letters, so one is a plausible outcome. Strict priority can starve the low class if high-priority traffic is continuous; a weighted share (for example one in ten polls serves a lower class) prevents it.

#### Problem 2: effectively-once delivery

The system is at-least-once: a worker can crash after calling the provider and before acknowledging the queue message, and the message will be delivered again. Four layers reduce duplicates for the user. The idempotency key rejects duplicate requests at intake. The router keys per-channel messages by `(notification id, channel)` and the channel worker checks the attempt table before sending. The request to the provider carries the same request id on every retry, which providers that support idempotent sends use to discard repeats. And the status update is conditional (`sent` only from `queued`). None of these is perfect: after a crash between the provider call and the attempt record, the worker cannot know whether the provider accepted the message, and one duplicate can occur; for critical messages a rare duplicate is preferable to a loss.

#### Problem 3: provider failures and rate limits

Providers throttle (HTTP 429 with a retry hint), time out or fail for minutes. The worker therefore uses a token bucket per provider and per credential, whose rate is the provider's contractual limit; exponential backoff with full jitter for retries (the delay is uniform between 0 and 2 to the power of the attempt in seconds, so that retries of many messages do not synchronise); a circuit breaker per provider that stops calls after consecutive failures; and a secondary provider for the channel, used when the breaker of the primary is open. Messages that cannot be sent wait in a delay queue and drain at a limited rate after recovery.

blocks.text:
#### Problem 4: campaigns

A campaign to 20 million users is not 20 million API calls. The campaign service reads the segment in pages, creates messages in batches, and enqueues them at the configured rate with the bulk priority, so that the queue does not hold the full set at once. Sending is spread over the user's local time (for example 09:00 in each time zone) when the content allows it, which also lowers the peak. Campaign messages carry a campaign id for per-campaign status counts and a kill switch that stops further enqueueing.

### Bottlenecks, failures and real-world problems

#### Bulk campaign delays critical messages

**Scenario.** A campaign of 20 million messages starts at 08:00; at 08:05 users request password reset codes. **Symptoms.** Codes arrive after 30 to 60 minutes; support tickets rise; the login failure rate rises.

**Diagnosis.** Queue lag per topic shows all traffic in one queue; the oldest message age of the critical class equals the campaign backlog. **Root cause.** Critical and bulk messages shared a queue and a worker pool.

**Fix.** Separate queues and worker capacity per priority, as in the simulation (median critical wait 36 s against 0 s), and cap the campaign's enqueue rate. **Prevention.** Alert on the oldest-message age per priority, with a hard target for critical messages, and load-test with a simultaneous campaign.

#### Duplicate notifications after a worker crash or producer retry

**Scenario.** A worker is killed after the provider accepted an SMS and before the queue acknowledgement; separately, a producer retries a request after a timeout. **Symptoms.** Users receive the same message twice; the duplicate rate follows deployments and timeouts.

**Diagnosis.** Group the attempt table by `(notification id, channel)`; two successful attempts reveal the redelivery, and two notification ids with the same business event reveal the producer retry. **Root cause.** At-least-once delivery without deduplication at each hop.

**Fix.** Require an idempotency key from producers, deduplicate at intake and at the channel worker, pass a stable request id to providers, and make status updates conditional. **Prevention.** Alert on the duplicate rate, and make graceful shutdown finish in-flight sends before acknowledgement.

#### Provider outage causes a retry storm

**Scenario.** The SMS provider returns errors for 25 minutes; every worker retries each message immediately, three times. **Symptoms.** Request rate to the provider triples, the provider returns 429, the account is throttled for longer, and the queue grows.

**Diagnosis.** Outbound request rate per provider rises while success rate falls; the retry count per message is high. **Root cause.** Retries without backoff, jitter or a circuit breaker amplify a partial failure into a full one.

**Fix.** Backoff with full jitter, a breaker that opens after consecutive failures (as in the outage diagram), a secondary provider, and a bounded retry budget per message (5 attempts, then dead-letter). **Prevention.** Track the ratio of retries to first attempts and alert when it exceeds a threshold such as 20%.

#### Invalid device tokens and poison messages

**Scenario.** After a large number of app uninstalls, 8% of push sends fail with "unregistered"; separately one template with a missing parameter throws an exception during rendering. **Symptoms.** The error rate and cost rise; a consumer partition stops advancing because the same message fails repeatedly.

**Diagnosis.** Error codes by provider response; a single message id appears again and again in the consumer logs. **Root** **cause.** Fatal errors were retried like transient ones, and a rendering failure was not isolated from the queue.

**Fix.** Classify results: remove tokens that the provider reports as invalid, mark fatal failures without retry, and move a message that fails rendering to the dead-letter queue after the retry limit so that the partition continues. **Prevention.** Validate templates against a schema at publish time, and review the dead-letter queue as an operational task.

### Trade-offs and extensions

- **Push, SMS or email.** SMS is the most expensive and the most reliable for reaching a phone without an app; push is cheap and fast but depends on the app and the device token; email is cheap and slow. A fallback chain (push first, SMS if undelivered after 60 seconds for critical messages) trades cost for reach.
- **Exactly once.** True exactly-once delivery to a third-party provider is impossible without provider support; the system offers deduplication and accepts rare duplicates for critical messages.
- **Synchronous versus asynchronous API.** A synchronous send gives the producer immediate status but couples its latency to the provider; the asynchronous API with a status endpoint and callbacks is preferred.
- **Ordering.** Messages to one user are not ordered across channels; where order matters (a status update sequence), include a sequence number and let the client display the newest.
- **Compliance.** Opt-outs and regulatory limits on marketing messages are enforced in the router, using the preference value at send time, with an audit record of each decision.

### Questions to expect

#### How do critical messages avoid waiting behind a campaign?

By separating them: distinct queues and worker capacity per priority, workers that poll the high queue first, and a rate cap on bulk enqueueing. The simulation shows a median wait of 0 s instead of 36 s.

#### How are duplicates prevented?

An idempotency key at intake, a unique `(notification id, channel)` at the channel worker, a stable request id passed to the provider, and conditional status updates. Rare duplicates remain possible after a crash between the provider call and the acknowledgement.

#### What happens when a provider is down?

Workers retry with exponential backoff and jitter, a circuit breaker stops calls after consecutive failures, a secondary provider takes over for the channel, and parked messages drain at a limited rate after recovery. Messages that exhaust their retries go to the dead-letter queue.

#### Why exponential backoff with jitter?

Backoff reduces the load on a failing provider, and jitter spreads the retries of many messages over time so that they do not arrive together at the same instants.

#### How are user preferences respected for queued messages?

Preferences are evaluated by the router at send time, not at intake, and checked again for bulk messages when they leave the delay queue.

#### How is a campaign to 20 million users sent without overloading anything?

The campaign service pages through the segment and enqueues at a configured rate with bulk priority; the channel workers' rate limiters enforce the provider limit; sending is spread across time zones; a kill switch stops the campaign.

#### How do delivery receipts work?

Providers call a webhook with their own message id and status; the callback handler authenticates the call, finds the attempt by provider message id and updates the status monotonically. Receipts can be late, duplicated or missing, so status is best effort and the system also times out `sent` messages.

#### How is the system scaled?

Partition topics by user id so that one user's messages are processed in order by one consumer, scale workers per channel independently, shard the log by user, and add providers per channel for capacity and redundancy.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Separate intake from delivery with queues, and separate priorities with distinct queues and worker capacity so that bulk messages never delay critical ones.
- Delivery is at-least-once; idempotency keys, per-channel dedup, stable provider request ids and conditional status updates give effectively-once behaviour.
- Retry with exponential backoff and full jitter, bound the attempts, use circuit breakers and a secondary provider, and dead-letter what cannot be delivered.
- Evaluate preferences and quiet hours at send time, and classify provider errors into transient and fatal.
- Campaigns are paced, paged and killable; the numbers (5,600 per second for 20 million in an hour) set the capacity.

A news feed presents each user with a ranked or chronological list of posts written by the accounts that user follows. The design problem is a read-heavy workload with a highly skewed write amplification: a single post by an account with many followers must become visible in many individual feeds within seconds, while a typical feed read must complete in tens of milliseconds. The central decision is where the work of assembling a feed is performed: at write time (fan-out on write), at read time (fan-out on read), or by a hybrid of both.

### Requirements and scope

#### Functional requirements

- A user publishes a post consisting of text and up to four media items.
- A user follows and unfollows other users.
- A user retrieves a home feed: the posts of followed accounts, newest first (ranked ordering is treated as an extension).
- The feed supports cursor-based pagination and an infinite scroll interaction.

#### Non-functional requirements

- Feed read latency: p99 below 200 ms for the first page, measured at the service boundary.
- Freshness: a post from a typical account appears in followers' feeds within 5 seconds; from a celebrity account within 30 seconds.
- Availability of the read path above 99.95 percent; the write path may degrade to queued acceptance.
- Eventual consistency of the feed is acceptable. A user must always see their own post immediately (read-your-writes for the author).

#### Out of scope

Ranking models, ad insertion, search, direct messages, content moderation pipelines, notifications, and analytics. These attach to the design through the event stream described below.

#### Assumptions

All volumes below are assumed for the purpose of sizing and are not measurements of any real service: 200 million daily active users (DAU), 10 feed opens per user per day, 0.5 posts per user per day, an average of 200 followers per account, and a heavy tail of accounts with more than 1 million followers.

### Capacity estimation

rows: 70,000 per s x 20 posts x 1 KB
`1.4 GB per s (11 Gbit per s),` `text only`
blocks.caption: Capacity estimate (all inputs assumed; peak factor 3 over the daily average).

blocks.text:
The estimate exposes the shape of the problem. Reads outnumber post writes by a factor of 20 (23,148 against 1,157 per second), but each write under a push model produces 200 cache inserts on average, so the cache absorbs about 10 times more insert operations than the number of feed reads it serves. The write amplification, not the read rate, is the scaling constraint; it also motivates keeping only identifiers (16 bytes per entry) in the cache rather than post bodies.

### API design

rows: `Header Idempotency-Key. Body: text, media_ids[].` `Response 201: post_id, created_at`
Retried requests with the same key return the original post\_id
Cursor is the last post\_id returned
blocks.caption: REST interface (all endpoints authenticated with a bearer token).

blocks.text:
Pagination uses a keyset cursor rather than an offset. Post identifiers are time-ordered 64-bit identifiers (snowflake-style), so "posts older than the cursor" is a stable predicate: new posts arriving at the head of the feed do not shift the pages already delivered, which an offset-based page number would do. The idempotency key on post creation protects against duplicate posts when a mobile client retries after a network timeout.

### Data model

blocks.text:
The follow relation is queried in two directions: "whom does this user follow" (pull path, ranking features) and "who follows this author" (fan-out). Each direction is stored as its own table with its own shard key, written together by the follow service. Posts are sharded by post\_id, which is a snowflake identifier, so that writes spread evenly and range scans by time remain possible within a shard. A sharded, replicated relational or wide-column store is appropriate here, as covered in the databases material; the design does not depend on the choice. The timeline is a Redis list per user holding at most 800 post identifiers, trimmed on every push. An entry is 16 bytes in the estimate (8 bytes post id, 4 bytes author id, 4 bytes flags). Per the 2013 description of Twitter's architecture on High Scalability, that system kept timelines in Redis with a maximum of 800 entries per user and retained only recently active users (a login within 30 days) in memory; the numbers here follow the same pattern but are otherwise assumptions.

### High-level architecture

blocks.text:
#### Write path

1. The client calls `POST /v1/posts`. The post service validates the request, assigns a snowflake identifier and inserts the row into the post store.
2. The post service publishes a `PostCreated` event to the fan-out queue, partitioned by author\_id so that the events of one author remain ordered.
3. A fan-out worker reads the author's follower list in pages of 1,000 and pushes the post identifier onto each follower's timeline (`LPUSH`, then `LTRIM` to 800). Accounts above the celebrity threshold are not fanned out; the event only updates the celebrity post index.
4. The service returns 201 as soon as step 1 and the queue publication succeed. Fan-out is asynchronous.

#### Read path

1. The client calls `GET /v1/feed`. The timeline service reads the user's list from the cache.
2. For every celebrity the user follows (a short list stored with the user), the service reads that author's recent posts from the celebrity index.
3. The identifiers are merged in descending order, the page boundary is applied using the cursor, and the post bodies, author profiles and counters are fetched in batch from the post store and its cache.
4. A cache miss (an inactive user) triggers a rebuild: the last 7 days of posts of followed accounts are read, merged and written back.

blocks.text:
### Deep dive

#### Fan-out on write, fan-out on read, or hybrid

blocks.caption: Comparison of feed assembly strategies.

blocks.text:
The decision is driven by the read to write ratio and by the follower distribution. Pure push is simplest to reason about and is the right choice when no account has more than a few thousand followers. Pure pull is acceptable for small systems. When the follower distribution has a heavy tail, the hybrid is the standard answer: push for the many, pull for the few. The threshold is a tunable, chosen by comparing the push cost saved against the read cost added.

#### Measuring the trade-off with a simulation

The following program builds a synthetic follow graph of 100,000 users, each following 50 accounts chosen with a power-law popularity (weight proportional to rank to the power of -0.8), and counts the timeline inserts per day (one post per user) and the post-store lookups per feed read for each strategy. The graph is synthetic and the counts are simulation results, not production measurements.

blocks.title: FanoutSim.java

blocks.code:
$ java FanoutSim.java
users=100000 follows/user=50 edges=5000000 max followers=67337
strategy              inserts/day (1 post each)  lookups per read
fan-out on write         5,000,000             1
fan-out on read            100,000             50
hybrid T=1000            3,787,498             13.13   (celebrities=363)
hybrid T=5000            4,390,792             7.09   (celebrities=47)
hybrid T=20000           4,745,358             3.55   (celebrities=7)
blocks.title: Run (JDK 21, seed fixed, output deterministic)

blocks.text:
What to notice: the most popular account has 67,337 followers, so one post under pure push costs 67,337 inserts. Raising the celebrity threshold from 1,000 to 20,000 followers reduces pull lookups per read from 13.13 to 3.55 but increases daily inserts from 3.79 million to 4.75 million. With the 20,000 threshold, 7 accounts are handled by pull, which removes the only accounts whose fan-out exceeds 20,000 inserts. The threshold is therefore a cost curve, and the operational choice is to select the point where the worst-case fan-out latency stays within the freshness target (see the failure scenarios below).

#### Timeline cache structure and rebuild

A Redis list supports `LPUSH` and `LTRIM` in constant time per element and returns a page with `LRANGE`. Its weakness is that a duplicate push produces a duplicate entry. A sorted set keyed by post\_id with the post\_id as score makes the insertion idempotent (`ZADD` of an existing member changes nothing) and allows range queries by cursor (`ZREVRANGEBYSCORE` below the cursor) at the cost of roughly twice the memory per entry. The design chooses the sorted set when the fan-out queue delivers at least once, which is the normal case; the list is a valid optimisation when duplicates are removed on read. Timelines of inactive users are evicted. When such a user returns, the cache miss path rebuilds the timeline from the follow list and the post store, bounded to the last 7 days and 800 entries. The rebuild is rate limited per shard so that a morning peak of returning users does not overload the post store.

#### Pagination and ranking

Chronological ordering needs no ranking service. When ranked ordering is added, the architecture becomes two-stage: the timeline cache supplies up to 800 candidates, a ranking service scores them with features read from a feature store, and the top page is returned. The cursor then refers to a ranking session identifier stored server-side for a short time, because the score order is not reproducible from a post\_id alone.

### Bottlenecks, failures and real-world problems
