blocks.text:
#### Celebrity fan-out storm

**Scenario.** An account with 50 million followers publishes a post. The fan-out workers begin 50 million inserts. **Symptoms.** Fan-out queue lag rises for all authors, because the partition holding the celebrity event is blocked; ordinary users report that their posts take minutes to appear. **Diagnosis.** The consumer lag metric per partition shows one partition far behind; the worker for that partition reports a single event in progress for several minutes. **Root** **cause.** Fan-out cost proportional to followers is applied uniformly, and one event occupies a partition worker serially. **Fix.** Exclude accounts above the threshold from push and serve them at read time through the celebrity index; for accounts near the threshold, split the follower list into chunks processed by a pool of workers in parallel. **Prevention.** Alert on the maximum fan-out duration, not the average; classify accounts automatically by follower count with hysteresis (promote at 100,000, demote at 80,000) to avoid flapping.

#### Stale entries after delete or unfollow

**Scenario.** A user deletes a post or a viewer unfollows an author. **Symptoms.** The deleted post still appears in followers' feeds; an unfollowed author continues to appear. **Diagnosis.** The identifier is present in the timeline cache but absent (or flagged deleted) in the post store. **Root cause.** The cache holds identifiers written in the past; removing them from every follower timeline is as expensive as the original fan-out. **Fix.** Treat the cache as a hint. Hydration reads the post store, and entries whose post is deleted, or whose author is no longer followed, are dropped from the page. Entries are physically removed lazily by the trim operation and the periodic rebuild. **Prevention.** Keep the hydration step mandatory and apply a block list and deletion flags at read time.

#### Cold cache after a cache cluster failure

**Scenario.** A cache shard group is lost and restarted empty. **Symptoms.** The post store CPU rises sharply, feed latency exceeds the objective, and error rates grow as rebuild requests queue. **Diagnosis.** The cache hit ratio drops to near zero for the affected shard range while rebuild queries dominate the post store. **Root cause.** Every returning user triggers an expensive rebuild simultaneously (a thundering herd on a cold cache). **Fix.** Rate limit rebuilds per shard, serve a degraded feed (the last 50 posts from the pull path) while rebuilding, and coalesce concurrent rebuilds of the same user. **Prevention.** Replicate the cache across availability zones, keep a rebuild budget as configuration, and test the cold start in a game day.

#### Duplicate fan-out

**Scenario.** A worker crashes after pushing to half of the followers and before committing its queue offset. **Symptoms.** After the restart, some followers see the same post twice. **Diagnosis.** Duplicate identifiers in a single user's timeline. **Root cause.** At-least-once delivery combined with a non-idempotent insert. **Fix.** Use an idempotent insert (sorted set keyed by post\_id) or de-duplicate on read. **Prevention.** Design every consumer in the pipeline as idempotent; commit offsets only after the work is complete.

### Trade-offs and extensions

- Push optimises read latency at the price of storage and write amplification; pull optimises write cost at the price of read latency. The hybrid adds an operational burden (threshold management and two code paths).
- Storing identifiers only keeps memory small but adds a hydration round trip on every read; caching hydrated post bodies in a separate cache reduces it.
- Ranked feeds require a feature store and an online ranker, and change the cursor semantics.
- Extension: following a hashtag or a topic is another graph edge type; the fan-out worker consults a generic subscription index instead of the follower table.
- Extension: multi-region deployment places a timeline cache per region, replicating post events asynchronously; a user reads from the nearest region and may observe cross-region lag of a few seconds.

### Questions to expect

#### Why not compute the feed at read time for everyone?

The read cost is O(followees) store queries plus a merge per request. At 70,000 peak reads per second and 200 followees, that is 14 million store queries per second. Push converts that into one cache read.

#### How is the celebrity threshold chosen?

By the fan-out latency target. If the pool performs 100,000 inserts per second and the freshness target is 30 seconds, the largest account that may be pushed has about 3 million followers; a threshold far below that (for example 100,000) leaves a safety margin and reduces wasted writes to inactive followers.

#### How does an author see their own post immediately?

The client inserts the post locally, and the timeline service additionally merges the author's own recent posts from the post store into the author's feed at read time, so read-your-writes holds without waiting for fan-out.

#### What happens to a follower who is offline for a week?

The timeline cache entry is evicted after the inactivity window. On return, the rebuild path reads recent posts of followed accounts; older posts are reachable by the pull path with pagination.

#### How is the ordering of posts guaranteed in the timeline?

Order follows the snowflake identifier, which encodes time. Events of one author remain ordered by partitioning the queue by author\_id; ordering across authors is by identifier and is approximate across clock skew of a few milliseconds.

#### How would the design change for 10 times the users?

The cache cluster grows linearly and is resharded with consistent hashing; the celebrity threshold is lowered; fan-out workers scale with queue partitions; post store shards are added. The design has no single global component except the identifier scheme, which is distributed.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Feed design is dominated by write amplification (followers per post), not by the raw read rate.
- Store identifiers in the timeline cache and hydrate from the post store; the cache is a hint, never the source of truth.
- Use push for ordinary accounts and pull for accounts above a follower threshold; derive the threshold from the fan-out latency target.
- Make every stage of the pipeline idempotent because the queue delivers at least once.
- Use keyset (cursor) pagination so that new posts do not shift delivered pages.

A chat system delivers short messages between users in near real time, keeps a durable conversation history, and tolerates devices that disconnect and reconnect at arbitrary times. The design problem differs from a feed in three ways: connections are long-lived and stateful, per-conversation ordering is visible to users, and the delivery state of every message (sent, delivered, read) is part of the product. The central decisions concern the connection layer, the source of message order, and the representation of delivery state.

### Requirements and scope

#### Functional requirements

- One-to-one conversations and group conversations (up to 1,024 members, assumed limit).
- Text messages and media attachments (media travels through object storage, not through the chat path).
- Delivery receipts: sent, delivered, read.
- Offline delivery: a message sent to an offline user is delivered after reconnection and a push notification is raised.
- Message history with pagination, available on every device of the user.

#### Non-functional requirements

- End-to-end latency below 200 ms at p99 between two online users in the same region.
- No message loss once the sender has received the server acknowledgement; no duplicates visible to the user.
- Messages of one conversation appear in the same order to all participants.
- Availability above 99.99 percent for message acceptance; delivery may be delayed during partial failures.

#### Out of scope

End-to-end encryption protocols (the server treats the payload as opaque bytes), voice and video calls, message search, bots, and spam detection.

#### Assumptions

Assumed volumes: 500 million DAU, 40 messages sent per user per day, 30 percent of DAU connected at the daily peak, an average of 1.3 recipients per message (a mixture of one-to-one and group traffic), 200 bytes per stored message including metadata.

### Capacity estimation

blocks.caption: Capacity estimate (all inputs assumed; peak factor 3).

blocks.text:
Two results shape the design. First, the number of heartbeats (5 million per second) exceeds the message rate by a factor of seven, so the connection layer must be optimised for idle connections: the gateway does no application work for a heartbeat and the heartbeat interval is a significant cost parameter. Second, the message bandwidth is small. The difficulty of chat is the number of connections and the state attached to them, not the data volume. The figure of 100,000 connections per node is an assumption that is achievable on tuned hardware with an event-driven server and about 10 KB of memory per connection (1 GB per node).

### API design

The primary channel is a WebSocket per device, carrying binary or JSON frames. Control operations that are not latency critical use REST.

blocks.text:
The messages table is the conversation log. Its partition key is conv\_id, so that one conversation resides on one replica set and a page of history is a single sequential read; its clustering key is seq in descending order. This layout suits a wide-column store with tunable consistency, as covered in the databases material, but a sharded relational store with the same keys is equivalent. The members table is partitioned by user\_id because the dominant query is "the conversations of this user". It carries the receipt state as two integers: `last_delivered_seq` and `last_read_seq`. A receipt for 5,000 unread messages is a single update of one integer instead of 5,000 row updates. A very active group could make one partition large. The usual remedy is a bucketed partition key (conv\_id plus a time bucket of, for example, one week), which bounds partition size while keeping a page of recent history within one or two partitions.

### High-level architecture

blocks.text:
#### Send and deliver flow

1. The sender app transmits a SEND frame over its WebSocket. The gateway forwards it to the chat service by gRPC; the gateway holds no conversation state.
2. The chat service obtains the conversation's next sequence number from its owning shard, appends the message to the message store with a quorum write, and only then returns the ACK carrying the sequence number. The sender displays one tick (sent).
3. The chat service reads the member list (cached), queries the session registry for the gateway of each online member, and sends one push RPC per gateway carrying the message and the list of local recipients.
4. The gateway writes the frame to each recipient connection. The recipient device acknowledges, and the chat service advances `last_delivered_seq`. A delivered receipt flows back to the sender.
5. When the recipient opens the conversation, the device sends RECEIPT(read, upto\_seq). The service updates `last_read_seq` and notifies the sender.

blocks.text:
#### Offline path

If the registry has no entry for a member, the message is already durable in the log. The chat service enqueues a push notification (APNs or FCM) containing only a wake-up hint. On reconnection the device sends SYNC for each conversation with the highest sequence it holds, or one inbox-level sync request listing its cursors. The server returns the missing range from the log. Because the log is the source of truth, no per-recipient offline queue is required.

blocks.text:
### Deep dive

#### Message ordering

rows: Clock skew reorders messages; trivially forged
Sort by arrival time at the receiving node
Skew between nodes; ties; concurrent senders reach different nodes
The owner is a serialisation point per conversation
blocks.caption: Alternatives for ordering messages within a conversation.

blocks.text:
Decision: a per-conversation sequence number assigned by the shard that owns the conversation. The serialisation point is acceptable because one conversation produces a small message rate (a very active group may produce tens of messages per second, far below the capacity of one shard). The owner is chosen by consistent hashing of conv\_id and replicated; a failover must not reuse sequence numbers, so the counter is persisted with the log or derived from the highest stored seq under the new owner. Sequence numbers make gap detection trivial: a client holding seq 10 that receives seq 12 knows that seq 11 is missing.

#### Verifying the ordering and deduplication logic

The following program implements the two halves of the protocol: a sequencer that deduplicates by client\_msg\_id, and a client receiver that buffers out-of-order frames, discards duplicates and detects gaps. The network is simulated by a fixed permutation of arrivals; this is a single-process simulation, not a network test.

blocks.title: ChatSim.java

blocks.code:
$ java ChatSim.java
retry returns same seq: true (seq 3)
arrive seq 3 -> pending=[3] lastShown=0
arrive seq 1 -> pending=[3] lastShown=1
arrive seq 1 -> pending=[3] lastShown=1
arrive seq 2 -> pending=[] lastShown=3
show seq 1: hello
  (drop duplicate seq 1)
show seq 2: hi, are you there?
show seq 3: meeting at 10
gap detected, client requests sync from seq 2
after resync lastShown=3 pending=[]
blocks.title: Run (JDK 21, deterministic)

blocks.text:
What to notice: the retried SEND returns the existing sequence number 3 rather than allocating 4; the client shows nothing for sequence 3 until sequences 1 and 2 have arrived; the duplicate of sequence 1 is dropped; and a lost frame is visible as a gap, which triggers a SYNC from the first missing sequence.

#### Receipts and group fan-out

Two storage strategies exist for delivering a group message.

headers: One inbox copy per member (write-time fan-out)
blocks.caption: Group message storage strategies.

blocks.text:
Chat history is shared and immutable apart from deletion flags, so the conversation log is stored once. Delivery fans out only over connections, never over storage: the chat service groups the online members of a group by gateway and sends one RPC per gateway. A group of 1,024 members spread over 300 gateways costs 300 RPCs, not 1,024. Read receipts in large groups are expensive in the UI as well as on the server; a common simplification is to disable per-member read receipts above a size (for example 100 members) and show only a count.

#### Connection management

Heartbeats detect dead connections: an interval of 30 seconds with a 3-interval timeout bounds the time during which the registry entry of a silently dead client is stale to 90 seconds. The session registry entry carries a time-to-live slightly above the timeout and is refreshed by heartbeats; an entry pointing to a failed gateway therefore expires on its own. A delivery RPC that fails because the gateway is unreachable removes the entry and takes the offline path.

### Bottlenecks, failures and real-world problems

blocks.text:
#### Reconnection storm

**Scenario.** A gateway node holding 100,000 connections is restarted during a deployment. **Symptoms.** Neighbouring gateways show a spike in new connections and TLS handshakes, CPU saturates, and the authentication service returns errors; reconnection attempts fail and repeat. **Diagnosis.** The new-connection rate per gateway rises from a few hundred per second to tens of thousands within one second and correlates with the restart time. **Root cause.** Clients reconnect immediately and in lockstep, and each reconnection performs authentication and a full sync. **Fix.** Clients apply exponential backoff with random jitter (for example uniform over 0 to 30 seconds for the first attempt). Gateways enforce an admission rate and answer excess connections with a retry-after value. Deployments drain connections gradually (a few percent per second) and send a reconnect hint before closing. **Prevention.** Load test node loss with realistic client behaviour; keep authentication tokens verifiable locally so that reconnection does not depend on a central call.

#### Stale session registry entry

**Scenario.** A gateway fails without cleanup; the registry still lists its users as connected. **Symptoms.** Messages to those users are pushed to a dead node, no delivered receipt arrives, and users report delayed messages although the log contains them. **Diagnosis.** Push RPCs time out for one gateway address; the registry holds entries with that address. **Root cause.** The registry is an optimistic cache of connection location and can be wrong. **Fix.** Time-to-live on entries; a delivery timeout that deletes the entry and falls back to the offline path; the push notification and the sync on reconnect remain the safety net. **Prevention.** Treat the registry as a hint, never as proof of delivery; delivery is confirmed only by a device acknowledgement.

#### Duplicate and out-of-order delivery

**Scenario.** A client retries a SEND after a timeout; a delivery RPC is retried after a gateway timeout. **Symptoms.** The same message appears twice, or messages appear in a different order on two devices. **Diagnosis.** Two stored rows with different seq and one client\_msg\_id, or frames with decreasing seq on a client. **Root cause.** At-least-once delivery without deduplication, and ordering based on arrival time. **Fix.** Deduplicate by (conv\_id, client\_msg\_id) at the sequencer and by seq at the client; order only by seq. **Prevention.** Property-test the protocol with injected duplication, reordering and loss, as the simulation above does in miniature.

#### Hot conversation partition

**Scenario.** A large public group receives thousands of messages per second after an event. **Symptoms.** The shard owning the conversation shows high CPU and write latency; other conversations on the same shard slow down. **Diagnosis.** Per-partition write rate far above the median; one conv\_id dominates. **Root cause.** All writes of a conversation serialise on one owner and one partition. **Fix.** Time-bucketed partitions, batching of sequence allocation (reserve ranges of 1,000 sequence numbers), and a read-only broadcast mode for very large channels where followers receive a feed-like stream. **Prevention.** Limit group size and message rate, and classify very large channels as a different product with a feed-style design.

### Trade-offs and extensions

- A per-conversation sequencer gives total order and simple gap detection but couples the availability of a conversation to its owner; replication and fast failover limit the effect.
- Cursor-based receipts reduce write cost by orders of magnitude but cannot express per-message receipts out of order.
- Multi-device support requires a per-device cursor and a per-device delivery state; the log is shared, so only cursors multiply.
- Presence and typing indicators are best-effort, ephemeral, and sent over the same connection with a short time-to-live and no durability; they must be throttled, since presence changes of large contact lists generate fan-out comparable to messages.
- End-to-end encryption moves the group fan-out of keys to the clients and prevents server-side search and spam inspection of content.

### Questions to expect

#### Why WebSocket and not HTTP polling?

Polling at a 5 second interval from 150 million clients is 30 million requests per second, nearly all empty. A WebSocket keeps one connection per client, with a heartbeat of 5 million per second at a 30 second interval and with no application work, and allows server push with latency of one network hop.

#### How does the server know which gateway holds a user?

Through a session registry (an in-memory key-value store) written by the gateway on connect and refreshed by heartbeats, with a time-to-live. It is a hint; a failed delivery falls back to the offline path.

#### How is message loss prevented?

The ACK is sent only after a quorum write to the log. The client retains unacknowledged messages and retries with the same client\_msg\_id. The recipient syncs from its last cursor, so any missed push is recovered from the log.

#### How are read receipts stored?

As a per-member cursor (`last_read_seq`). Per-message state is derived by comparing the message seq with the cursor.

#### How does the design scale a conversation beyond one shard?

A single conversation is not split; the throughput of one owner suffices for realistic groups. For very large channels the design changes to a broadcast model with fan-out on read.

#### What happens on a network partition between gateway and chat service?

The gateway cannot forward SEND, so the client does not receive an ACK and retries after reconnecting to another gateway; the idempotency key prevents duplicates. Deliveries to users of the isolated gateway time out and take the offline path.

#### How is the order across devices of the same user kept consistent?

All devices read the same log ordered by seq; each device keeps its own cursor and local send queue. A message sent from device A appears on device B through the normal delivery path with its sequence number.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Chat load is dominated by connection count and heartbeats, not by bytes; size the gateway tier by connections per node.
- Order messages with a per-conversation sequence assigned by the owning shard; never by client or arrival time.
- Acknowledge the sender after the durable write; deduplicate with a client-generated message id; confirm delivery with a device acknowledgement.
- Store each message once per conversation and represent receipts as cursors per member.
- Treat the session registry as a hint, and protect gateways from reconnection storms with jitter and admission control.
